findings.title: Server-Side JavaScript injection via eval() on contribution amounts
findings.attack_path: Authenticated user POSTs preTax/afterTax/roth to /contributions; handler calls eval() directly on each raw string before validation, so a payload such as 'global.process.mainModule.require("child_process").execSync("id")' executes in the Node process. Achieves remote code execution on the app server, enabling DB credential theft and lateral movement to MongoDB.
findings.remediation: Replace eval() with parseInt()/Number() parsing of the three fields and reject NaN; never pass request data to eval/Function. The fix is already commented in app/routes/contributions.js.

findings.title: NoSQL/server-side JS injection via $where on allocations threshold
findings.attack_path: Authenticated user requests /allocations/:userId?threshold=...; getByUserIdAndThreshold interpolates the raw threshold string into a Mongo $where clause ($where: this.userId == X && this.stocks > 'THRESHOLD'). Payloads like 0';while(true){} (DoS) or 1'; return true;// (data exfiltration of all allocations) run as JavaScript inside the MongoDB server.
findings.remediation: Eliminate $where; validate threshold with parseInt and a numeric range check, and use a structured comparison query ({stocks:{$gt:n}}). Fix is commented in app/data/allocations-dao.js.

findings.title: Passwords stored and compared in plaintext
findings.attack_path: addUser writes the raw password to the users collection; validateLogin compares fromDB === fromUser. Any read access to MongoDB (via TM-001/TM-002 RCE, a misconfigured/exposed instance, or a backup) yields every user's cleartext credential, enabling account takeover and credential reuse across systems. bcrypt-nodejs is a dependency but the hashing path is commented out.
findings.remediation: Hash passwords with bcrypt.hashSync(password, genSalt) on signup and bcrypt.compareSync on login; migrate existing records on next login. Code is present-but-disabled in app/data/user-dao.js.

findings.title: Sensitive PII (SSN, DOB, bank account/routing) stored unencrypted
findings.attack_path: Profile updates persist ssn, dob, bankAcc, bankRouting as cleartext in users. The encryption helper in profile-dao.js is commented out. With any DB read primitive (TM-001/TM-002) or an exposed Mongo port, an attacker exfiltrates regulated financial PII for all users in bulk.
findings.remediation: Encrypt ssn/dob/bank fields at rest (the commented crypto helpers, with a per-record random IV and a KMS-managed key) and enforce TLS to MongoDB; restrict DB network exposure.

findings.title: Server-Side Request Forgery via attacker-controlled research URL
findings.attack_path: GET /research?url=<attacker>&symbol=<x> builds url = req.query.url + req.query.symbol and passes it to needle.get, then streams the raw response body back to the client. An attacker targets cloud metadata (http://169.254.169.254/...) or internal services and reads the response, enabling credential theft and internal pivot.
findings.remediation: Remove the user-supplied url; pin the upstream provider host server-side, allow-list schemes/hosts, block link-local/RFC1918 ranges, and never echo the raw upstream body.

findings.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference on /allocations/:userId
findings.attack_path: displayAllocations takes userId from the URL path param instead of req.session, with no ownership check. Any logged-in user iterates /allocations/1, /allocations/2, ... to read every other user's allocation and identity (name) data. Horizontal authorization bypass.
findings.remediation: Derive userId from req.session.userId (the commented fix), and add an explicit ownership/authorization check in the handler.

findings.title: Missing function-level access control on admin Benefits feature
findings.attack_path: Routes /benefits (GET/POST) are guarded only by isLoggedIn, not isAdmin (the isAdmin guard is commented out). The handler also hardcodes user.isAdmin:true in the view context. Any authenticated non-admin user lists all non-admin users and alters their benefitStartDate, a privileged HR operation.
findings.remediation: Add the isAdmin middleware to both /benefits routes (the commented variant in app/routes/index.js) and stop forcing isAdmin:true in the rendered context.

findings.title: Stored Cross-Site Scripting via memos rendered to all users
findings.attack_path: POST /memos stores req.body.memo verbatim in a shared collection; /memos renders every memo via marked(doc.memo) into a page with Swig autoescape disabled. marked.setOptions({sanitize:true}) is set but marked 0.3.5 sanitization is bypassable, and raw HTML/script in a memo executes in every other viewer's session, including potential admins, yielding session/cookie theft and account takeover.
findings.remediation: Enable Swig autoescape, upgrade/replace marked with a maintained sanitizer (e.g. DOMPurify on rendered output), set httpOnly+Secure session cookies, and add CSP.

findings.title: Reflected/stored XSS through disabled template autoescaping (profile, error, login)
findings.attack_path: swig.setDefaults({autoescape:false}) disables output encoding globally. Profile fields (ssn, address, bankAcc, lastName), the error-template {{error}}, and login {{userName}} render untrusted values without encoding. The website field is HTML-encoded for one context but reused as an href, and the profile link uses firstNameSafeString as an href, allowing javascript: URI injection. Stored values fire in the victim's own and other sessions.
findings.remediation: Set autoescape:true; encode per output context (HTML body vs. URL attribute vs. JS); use ESAPI encodeForURL for href contexts.

findings.title: Default/seed accounts with weak, predictable credentials
findings.attack_path: db-reset.js seeds admin/Admin_123 (isAdmin:true) plus user1/User1_123 and user2/User2_123 in cleartext, and app.json/Docker run db-reset on deploy. An attacker logs in with the known admin password to obtain full administrative access; signup password policy (1-20 any chars) does not prevent weak passwords either.
findings.remediation: Remove seed users from production deploy, force a strong unique admin password at first run, and enforce a real password policy (the commented PASS_RE in session.js).

findings.title: Hardcoded session secret and crypto key committed in source
findings.attack_path: config/env/all.js hardcodes cookieSecret 'session_cookie_secret_key_here' and cryptoKey 'a_secure_key_for_crypto_here'. Anyone with repo access (public OWASP repo) knows the session-signing secret and can forge/predict session cookies for arbitrary userIds, bypassing authentication; the same applies to any data encrypted with the static crypto key (also static-IV via config.iv).
findings.remediation: Load secrets from environment/secret manager, rotate them, and remove from VCS; use a random per-deploy secret and per-record random IV.

findings.title: TLS private key and certificate committed to the repository
findings.attack_path: artifacts/cert/server.key (a 1024-bit RSA private key) and server.crt are committed. Anyone with repo read access holds the private key; if this cert were used for TLS, an attacker could decrypt captured traffic or impersonate the server (MITM). The 1024-bit key length is itself below modern strength.
findings.remediation: Revoke and rotate the key, remove it from git history, generate a fresh 2048-bit+ key managed outside VCS, and provision certs at deploy time.

findings.title: ReDoS via catastrophic backtracking in bank-routing validation regex
findings.attack_path: handleProfileUpdate tests bankRouting against /([0-9]+)+\#/. The nested + quantifier causes exponential backtracking on inputs like a long run of digits with no trailing '#'. A single authenticated POST /profile with such a string pins a CPU core and, because Node is single-threaded, stalls the whole event loop (full DoS).
findings.remediation: Use the linear regex /([0-9]+)\#/ (the commented fix), bound input length, and consider a non-backtracking validator.

findings.title: Missing rate limiting / account lockout on login enables brute force and credential stuffing
findings.attack_path: POST /login has no rate limiting, no lockout, and returns distinct 'Invalid username' vs 'Invalid password' messages (username enumeration). Combined with weak/known seed passwords (TM-010), an attacker enumerates valid accounts then brute-forces/stuffs credentials at high speed.
findings.remediation: Add per-account and per-IP rate limiting plus lockout/backoff, return a single generic error for both cases (the commented fix in session.js), and add monitoring/alerting on failed logins.

findings.title: No CSRF protection on state-changing POST routes
findings.attack_path: csurf is a dependency but app.use(csrf()) is commented out; templates emit {{csrftoken}} that is never populated. With cookie-based sessions and no SameSite/CSRF token, a victim visiting an attacker page is forced to submit /profile, /contributions, /benefits, or /memos, changing financial data or planting stored XSS in their authenticated context.
findings.remediation: Enable csurf middleware, populate res.locals.csrftoken, validate tokens on every state-changing route, and set SameSite=Lax/Strict on the session cookie.

findings.title: Open redirect via /learn?url= parameter
findings.attack_path: GET /learn does res.redirect(req.query.url) with no validation. An attacker crafts /learn?url=https://evil.example/phish; the trusted app domain redirects victims to a phishing or token-stealing site, lending credibility to the lure.
findings.remediation: Validate the redirect target against an allow-list of internal paths, or drop the parameter and redirect to a fixed resource.

findings.title: Session fixation: session ID not regenerated on login
findings.attack_path: handleLoginRequest sets req.session.userId without calling req.session.regenerate() (signup does regenerate, login does not). An attacker who fixes a victim's session id (e.g. over plaintext HTTP, TM-019) before login retains a valid authenticated session afterward.
findings.remediation: Call req.session.regenerate() on successful login before assigning userId (the documented fix in session.js).

findings.title: Insecure session cookie flags (httpOnly/secure/SameSite unset, persistent uninitialized sessions)
findings.attack_path: express-session is configured with saveUninitialized:true, resave:true, no cookie.httpOnly, no cookie.secure, no SameSite, and the default 'connect.sid' name. Cookies are readable by injected JS (chains with TM-008/TM-009 to steal sessions) and transmitted over plaintext HTTP, and the default MemoryStore is not production-safe.
findings.remediation: Set cookie {httpOnly:true, secure:true, sameSite:'lax', maxAge}, set saveUninitialized:false, use a persistent session store, and rename the cookie.

findings.title: Application served over plaintext HTTP (no TLS, no HSTS)
findings.attack_path: server.js starts http.createServer (the https branch is commented). All traffic, including login credentials, session cookies, SSN and bank data, crosses the network in cleartext. A network attacker (shared Wi-Fi, on-path) sniffs credentials/sessions and can MITM/inject responses.
findings.remediation: Terminate TLS (https.createServer or a TLS-terminating proxy), redirect HTTP->HTTPS, enable HSTS via helmet, and set Secure cookies.

findings.title: Missing security HTTP headers (helmet disabled): no CSP, no X-Frame-Options, no nosniff, x-powered-by leak
findings.attack_path: The entire helmet block is commented out and x-powered-by is not disabled. No Content-Security-Policy (amplifies the XSS in TM-008/TM-009), no frameguard (clickjacking on authenticated pages), no MIME nosniff, and the Express version is advertised, aiding targeted exploitation of known CVEs.
findings.remediation: Enable helmet (CSP, frameguard, noSniff, HSTS), disable x-powered-by, and tune CSP to block inline script.

findings.title: Verbose error handler leaks stack traces to clients
findings.attack_path: errorHandler renders error-template.html with the raw {{error}} object (and autoescape is off). Triggering an exception returns internal details, paths, and stack fragments that aid an attacker mapping the system; the unescaped error also re-introduces an XSS sink if attacker-influenced text reaches it.
findings.remediation: Return a generic error page to clients, log full detail server-side only, and escape any displayed value.

findings.title: Log injection / forging via unsanitized username in console logs
findings.attack_path: On a failed login, session.js logs the raw userName with no CRLF sanitization. An attacker submits a username containing newlines/control chars to forge fabricated log lines, hide their activity, or break downstream log parsers/SIEM (defeating accountability).
findings.remediation: Encode/sanitize user input before logging (strip CRLF, the commented ESAPI fix), and use structured logging.

findings.title: NoSQL operator injection on login/lookup via untyped request body
findings.attack_path: validateLogin/getUserByUserName pass req.body.userName straight into usersCol.findOne({userName}). bodyParser.json() lets an attacker send a JSON body where userName is an object such as {"$gt":""} or {"$ne":null}; the query then matches an arbitrary user document. Combined with plaintext password compare logic this enables authentication bypass / unintended record selection.
findings.remediation: Coerce userName/password to strings (typeof checks) before querying, or use a query sanitizer (e.g. mongo-sanitize) and parameterize equality strictly.

findings.title: Mass assignment / unrestricted benefit date and HPP on profile update
findings.attack_path: updateBenefits writes client-supplied benefitStartDate to any userId with no validation, and profile/contributions handlers consume request fields without type checks (HTTP Parameter Pollution can turn a string field into an array, breaking string ops and causing errors/DoS as flagged in profile.js comments). Untrusted structured input reaches Mongo $set unchecked.
findings.remediation: Validate and whitelist editable fields, enforce types on every body field, and reject array/object values where scalars are expected.

findings.title: Outdated and vulnerable dependencies (supply-chain risk)
findings.attack_path: package.json pins old releases (marked 0.3.5 with known XSS/ReDoS, mongodb 2.x driver, swig 1.4.2 unmaintained, express 4.13.x, needle 2.2.4) and uses tarball/git dependencies. Known CVEs in these transitive components are reachable from the memos (marked) and research (needle) surfaces, and the build pulls unpinned/floating versions (grunt-env latest), widening supply-chain exposure.
findings.remediation: Run npm audit, upgrade to maintained versions, pin exact versions, replace abandoned packages (swig), and add SCA scanning to CI.

findings.title: CI/CD and container supply-chain weaknesses (floating images, dev creds, no chown in prod)
findings.attack_path: Dockerfile uses mutable node:12-alpine and leaves the production chown/permission-hardening line commented; docker-compose runs db-reset (wiping/seeding data) on every start; CI checks out at floating action tags and runs the seeded test instance. A compromised base image, registry, or action tag injects code into the deployed artifact, and the seed step can clobber data if pointed at a real DB.
findings.remediation: Pin base images and GitHub Action SHAs, enable the prod permission-hardening, run as non-root, gate db-reset to non-prod, and add image/dependency scanning.
